transcript.content: Hello, I’m Dr. AI. What brings you in today?

Lately I keep losing important things for my catering and church work—papers, lists, even ingredients—and it’s starting to mess up events I’m responsible for. It's gotten to the point where it's really affecting my confidence, so I wanted to get it checked out.

Did these attention and forgetfulness problems start in childhood or have they only begun recently? Also, do you feel mainly distracted and disorganized, or are you also having persistent worry, low mood, or memory problems that are new for you?

These problems actually go back to childhood—my elementary school teachers always said I was bright but constantly daydreaming and losing my homework. It has just become much more of a struggle over the last 11 months since I retired and took on more catering and church responsibilities. I feel healthy and well-rested otherwise, so it's really about being distracted and disorganized rather than feeling depressed, anxious, or having a completely new memory issue.
Besides being distracted and disorganized, do you also often feel restless, fidgety, interrupt others, or act before thinking?

No, I don't really feel restless, fidgety, or impulsive like that. My difficulties are almost entirely related to losing my focus, getting distracted, and forgetting where I put things or what I was supposed to do.
Before age 12, did these attention problems happen in more than one setting, such as at school and at home, and did they cause clear problems with grades, behavior, or completing tasks?

Yes, it definitely happened both at school and at home. My elementary school teachers would tell my parents I was bright but always daydreaming and losing my homework, and at home I'd constantly forget my chores. It caused a lot of issues because I just couldn't follow through on instructions unless someone stood right over me to make sure I did them.

latest_inference.note: Previously the only candidate was F90.0, and the interview now strongly supports that it remains the best fit: the inattention and disorganization began in childhood, occurred in more than one setting, and caused clear functional impairment. Hyperactivity/impulsivity are not prominent, which makes a predominantly inattentive presentation more likely than other attention or mood/anxiety-related conditions. No new evidence suggests an alternative ICD-10 diagnosis, so the candidate list remains the same.

More history is needed about childhood onset, duration, mood/anxiety symptoms, and any medical or substance causes.

final_diagnosis.reason: The presentation is most consistent with ADHD, predominantly inattentive type: lifelong inattention/disorganization beginning in childhood, symptoms present in more than one setting (school and home), and current functional impairment in work-related responsibilities. Hyperactivity/impulsivity is denied, and there is no evidence that anxiety, depression, or a new memory disorder better explains the symptoms.
